Mamtazuddin Ahmed with Saifuddin Ahmed Chowdhury, Advocates ----- For the Petitioners. 
SK Sinha, Advocate  ----- For the Opposite Party.
parties:
Sher Mohammad & another ----- Petitioners.
Vs.
Sarada Bala Sen and another ----- Opposite Party.
full_judgment:
This Rule obtained under section 115 of the Code of Civil Procedure is directed against an order dated 23.3.92 passed by Mr. Md. Aminul Islam, First Additional Assistant Judge, Sadar, Chittagong, in Other Suit No. 7 of 1991. 

 2. Facts, as stated in the petition, in short, are, that the plaintiff opposite party No. 1 instituted a suit, being Other Suit No. 220 of 1978 for ejectment of a tenant, for arrear of rent and compensation. The suit was renumbered as Other Suit No. 40/90 and ultimately when it was transferred to the Additional Assistant Judge, First Court, Sadar, Chittagong, for disposal it was renumbered as other Suit No. 7 of 1991. 

 3. In the plaint the plaintiff claims that the defendant Haradan Chowdhury has been his monthly tenant since 1st November, 1974, at a monthly rent of Taka 125.00. Since July, 1975 the defendant defaulted in paying rent and as the plaintiff had a bonafide requirement of the premises he served a notice under section 106 of the Transfer of Property Act, terminating the tenancy from July, 1978. The defendant received the notice yet failed to hand over the vacant possession of the suit land. Hence the suit. 

 4. The defendant opposite party No. 2 contested the suit by denying the relationship of landlord and tenant with the plaintiff. He claims that in 1972 he entered into the premises as monthly tenant of one Parimal Bhattacherjee who later on sold his interest to Abdus Salam and others and from July 1970 he was attorned to the said Abdus Salam. 

 5. On 9.2.92 the petitioners submitted an application claiming that the plaintiff is not the owner of the suit premises. They purchased it from Abdus Salam and others, and the defendant since then paid them rent which has been increased from time to time. They further claim to have instituted a title suit, being Title Suit No. 52/87, regarding the suit premises in the court of Subordinate Judge, First Court, Sadar, Chittagong, in which the plaintiff of Other Suit No. 7 of 1991 has been made the defendant No. 2. The latter appeared in that case by submitting written statement, but did not mention anything in Other Suit No. 7 of 1991 about the pendency of the Title Suit No. 52 of 1987. 

 6. The petitioners further claim that the plaintiff is not entitled to evict the defendant and the petitioners are entitled to be impleaded as defendants as they are the owners of the suit premises. It the suit is disposed of without their being added as parties it will affect their title and also the result of Title Suit No. 52 of 1987. The petition was rejected by the learned Additional Assistant Judge on the ground that there is no legal basis for adding the petitioners as parties. 

 8. Mr. Momtazuddin Ahmed, the learned Advocate for the petitioners, submits that the impugned order was passed on wrong conception of law. By denying to add the petitioners as parties the trial Court has excluded necessary and proper parties from appearing in the suit. In their absence there will be no effective and proper adjudication of all questions involved in the suit. More so, when the defendant tenant has denied the title of the plaintiff and set up the petitioners as landlord. He submits that as a result of the defendant's claim the suit has lost its simple character of being an ejectment suit and now" involves adjudication of title incidentally and the court is authorised to go into the title incidentally. " Unless the petitioners are impleaded the plaintiff who has no title may get a decree and thereby prejudice the petitioners title to the suit premises. In support of the petitioners claim that they are necessary and proper parties the learned Advocate has cited the cases of Mst. Jahanara Begum Vs. AL Md. Shamsul Haque reported in 27 DLR (AD) 129 in which the general principles of who is a necessary party has been discussed. 

 9. Mr. SK Sinha, the learned Advocate for the appellant opposite party, submits that, on the other hand if the petitioners are allowed to be added then it will result in a multiplicity of suits involving numerous questions of law and fact, and the transformation of a simple suit into a title suit, in which case there will be no end to the dispute. He also submits that an eviction proceeding under section 18 of the Premises Rent Control Ordinance is more or less a summary proceeding in nature and in such a suit a third party should not be added. In support of his above submissions he has cited the following cases; 1977 AIR, Orissa 184, 1925 AIR Calcutta 26, AIR 1960 Bombay 238, 1978 AIR Jammu and Kashmir 85, AIR, Nagpur 234, 42 DLR page 72 and 1983 BLD 274. 

 "The Court may at any stage of the proceedings, either upon or without the application of either party, and on such terms as may appear to the court to be just, order that the name of any party improperly joined, whether as plaintiff or defendant, be struck out, and that the name of any person who ought to have been joined, whether as plaintiff or defendant, or whose presence before the Court may be necessary in order to enable the Court effectually and completely to adjudicate upon and settle all the questions involved in the suit, be added." 

 11. This confers a discretion upon the Court and which discretion should be exercised taking into consideration the facts and circumstances of a particular litigation, subject to the general principle that the parties cannot be added if it actually changes or alters the nature of the suit. Hingu Lal Vs. Baldeo Ram 1902, 24 All ER 53. 

 12. Besides, only in two cases may a person be added as a party to a suit. First, when an effective decree cannot be passed without making him a party and secondly, when the suit cannot be effectively and completely decided without his presence. Mst. Jahanara Begum Vs. ML Md. Shamsul Hoque, 27 DLR (AD) 129. 

 14. This passage is actually referring to a case where the precedent title of a third party is not disputed. Apart from that, the passage strictly speaking, will imply that only all those persons who are in physical possession of the suit property should be made defendants and others are neither necessary nor proper parties. 

 15. From the above discussion it appears that in an ejectment suit, if the plaintiff can make out a legal title to land, he is entitled to maintain a suit against the person in actual juridical possession of such land as such person is the only necessary and proper party. A third party will not be added if it transforms the nature of the suit from a simple rent suit into a complex title suit. But it does not mean that the question of title may not be investigated incidentally, as for example, it may be investigated in a suit for arrears of rent where the tenant defendant disputes the extent of title of the plaintiff to the arrears demanded, making it incumbent on the court to determine the point before the claim is allowed or disallowed. 

 16. In the instant case the petitioners are neither proper parties nor necessary parties. Nowhere in the plaint the cause of action against them has been disclosed. I do not see any allegation that prior to the suit filed by the plaintiff in 1978, the petitioners set up a claim in the suit premises. The Title Suit No. 52/87 comes after the ejectment suit was filed by the petitioners in 1978. Then again their application to be added as parties was made at a stage when the case was ready for argument after closing of evidence. If the petitioners' claim to be the land owners is genuine then naturally they would have known about the suit from the defendant-tenant earlier and would not have waited till such a late stage to apply to the court to be added as parties. 

 17. Moreover, if the petitioners are now allowed to be impleaded then the plaintiffs simple suit for recovery of rent and eviction of the defendant-tenant will be transformed into a complex title suit between the plaintiff and the defendants along with the petitioners, and the relief asked for in the original suit will pale into secondary importance. In this connection I have also considered the decision held in the case of Nurul Akbar and others Vs. Saifur Ahmed and others BSCR 1979 page 3 referred to by Mr. Momtazuddin Ahmed, the learned Advocate for the petitioners, wherein a stranger is allowed to be added as a party in an ejectment suit. But that decision, in my opinion, is not attracted in the instant case as the facts are quite different in the said case the plaintiff filed an ejectment suit against the sole defendant claiming her to be a temporary monthly tenant and alleged that the defendant was holding over the property even after the expiry of the lease. The defendant denied a landlord-tenant relationship and claimed adverse possession from the time of her predecessor, Ram Chandra Roy, from whom she has purchased the suit land, then had her name mutated in the Municipal Register and later on sold the suit land to the third party who filed an application to be added in the suit. The Appellate Division of the Supreme Court allowed the third party to be added as party as the court below came to the findings that the third party had purchased the property and had been in possession. But in the instant case the petitioners are neither in possession of the suit premises nor have their ownership been established. The ownership has remained very much a disputed fact and therefore I am of the opinion that they are not necessary and proper parties in this suit for ejectment. 

 18. Apart from this consideration, the petitioners have themselves filed Title Suit No. 52 of 1987 in the court of the Subordinate Judge, First Court, Sadar, Chittagong, claiming title to the suit premises. The plaintiff has been made a party in that suit. Even if the petitioners are not impleaded in the instant case any decision held therein will not in any manner bind or affect the right, title or interest of the petitioners in the suit premises. The petitioners' right in Title Suit No. 52 of 1987 will be decided without being prejudiced or influenced in any manner by the decision in Other Suit No. 7 of 1991. 

 20. No doubt the impugned order is a very sketchy one. It merely states that the application stands rejected as there is no 'legal basis' for adding the petitioners' as parties. There should have been more application of mind by the learned Additional Assistant Judge. Under Order 1 rule 10 the court has first to be satisfied as to the conditions mentioned in the said Order before an order is given as to whether a person is to be added or not The learned Additional Assistant Judge is required to express his opinion, one way or the other, as to whether addition of the petitioners as parties would be necessary in order to enable the court effectually and completely to adjudicate upon and settle all the questions involved in the suit. However because of the nature of the suit i.e. it is an ejectment suit under section 19 of the Premises Rent Control Ordinance I am not inclined to send the case to the trial Court on remand. Moreover, the learned Additional Assistant Judge has at least given a reason for rejecting the application, however sketchy it may be, and the reason is that there is "no legal basis" for adding the petitioners as parties. I do not think it will serve ends of justice if the case is sent to the trial Court on remand on this point alone. 

 21. Mr. Momtazuddin Ahmed, the learned Advocate for the petitioner, further argues that the defendant has denied the title of the plaintiff even before the notice under sec. 106 of the Transfer of Property Act had been served upon him. By such prior denial the defendant has caused the determination of tenancy by forfeiture, consequently the ejectment suit is not maintainable. But I do not have any evidence before me which supports the claim that such prior denial of tenancy was made. The defendant appears to have denied the title of the plaintiff for the first time in the written statement. 

 22. In view of the decision in Ahmed Hussain Vs. Zakia Khatun, 20 DLR 1157 it will appear that denial of the title of the plaintiff landlord in the written statement of a suit is not available as a ground for forfeiture, obviously for the reason that the suit was filed before the written statement and disclaimer or the challenge of the title of the plaintiff was made in the written statement. Therefore, the denial of the title of the plaintiff in the written statement will not be available under section 111(g) (2) of the Transfer of Property Act, causing the determination of tenancy by forfeiture.
